cards.front: M-715 official READING vocabulary: which words can appear in the read-aloud sentences of the English reading test?
cards.back:
READING vocabulary (all words that can appear in the read-aloud sentences) — M-715 (01/10) verbatim:
PEOPLE: Abraham Lincoln · George Washington
CIVICS: American flag · Bill of Rights · capital · citizen · city · Congress · country · Father of Our Country · government · President · right · Senators · state/states · White House
PLACES: America · United States · U.S.
HOLIDAYS: Presidents' Day · Memorial Day · Flag Day · Independence Day · Labor Day · Columbus Day · Thanksgiving

VERBS: can · come · do/does · elects · have/has · is/are/was/be · lives/lived · meet · name · pay · vote · want
OTHER (FUNCTION): a · for · here · in · of · on · the · to · we
OTHER (CONTENT): colors · dollar bill · first · largest · many · most · north · one · people · second · south

cards.back: PEOPLE: Adams · Lincoln · Washington. PLACES: Alaska · California · Canada · Delaware · Mexico · New York City · United States · Washington · Washington, D.C.
cards.memory_hook: Capital letters matter on names: Washington, Lincoln, Adams, and the place names all start with a capital.

cards.front: WRITING test — which CIVICS words can be dictated?
cards.back: American Indians · capital · citizens · Civil War · Congress · Father of Our Country · flag · free · freedom of speech · President · right · Senators · state/states · White House.

cards.front: WRITING test — which MONTHS, VERBS, and content words can be dictated?
cards.back: MONTHS: February · May · June · July · September · October · November. VERBS: can · come · elect · have/has · is/was/be · lives/lived · meets · pay · vote · want. Content: blue · white · red · taxes · dollar bill · first · one hundred/100 · people · north · south.
cards.memory_hook: Months always start with a capital. Watch the writing-only content words: taxes, red/white/blue, dollar bill.

source_ref.ref: USCIS M-715 reading/writing vocabulary

cards.front: WRITING practice — you hear: "Washington was the first President." Write it.
cards.back: Correct: Washington was the first President. Common misses: lowercase 'president' or 'washington'; misspelling Washington. Capitalize names and President.
cards.memory_hook: Name + was + the first + President. Two capitals to remember: Washington and President.

source_ref.ref: USCIS M-715 reading/writing vocabulary

cards.front: WRITING practice — you hear: "Citizens can vote." Write it.
cards.back: Correct: Citizens can vote. Common misses: 'citisens', no capital at the start, 'votes'. Start with a capital, simple present 'vote'.
cards.memory_hook: Three words. Capital C, simple verb 'vote' — not 'votes'.

source_ref.ref: USCIS M-715 reading/writing vocabulary

cards.front: WRITING practice — you hear: "The President lives in the White House." Write it.
cards.back: Correct: The President lives in the White House. Common misses: 'white house' lowercase; 'live' instead of 'lives'. Capitalize President and White House.
cards.memory_hook: Capitalize the two proper-ish terms: President and White House.

source_ref.ref: USCIS M-715 reading/writing vocabulary

cards.front: How perfect does my spelling and capitalization have to be?
cards.back: The officer is checking whether you can communicate — minor spelling or capitalization slips that DON'T change the meaning are generally acceptable. A word so misspelled it can't be understood, or a wrong word, does not count. Aim to be clear, not flawless.
cards.memory_hook: Goal: be understood. Small slips that keep the meaning are usually fine; unreadable or wrong words are not.

source_ref.ref: USCIS M-715 reading/writing vocabulary

cards.front: How should I practice the writing test?
cards.back: Write by hand on paper — print or cursive, whichever is clearer for you. Practice writing each official word and the practice sentences until they're automatic. You write only ONE dictated sentence correctly to pass the writing portion.
cards.memory_hook: Practice by hand, not just by reading. One correct sentence passes the writing part.

source_ref.ref: USCIS M-715 reading/writing vocabulary

recap_hooks.text: Make, carry out, explain — legislative writes the law, the executive (the President) carries it out, the judicial explains it: Congress, president, the courts.
Re-public: the public picks representatives. The market stays free — capitalism. Nobody is above the law. And three branches so no one grows too strong.
Supreme law? The Constitution. You change it with amendments — say it aloud: twenty-seven. And the Bill of Rights protects everyone LIVING here.
The Declaration DECLARES freedom — Life, Liberty, the pursuit of Happiness; equality and natural rights are its big ideas.
Senators: Six years, State-wide, two per state, one hundred total. Representatives: Run often, two years, district seats, four hundred thirty-five.

President maths: four, two, twenty-two. Then run the chain: Commander in Chief? The President. Signs bills? The President. Vetoes? The President. Appoints judges? The President. And the Cabinet advises.
Court maths: nine sit, five decide, robes for life — independent of politics. The highest court is the Supreme Court.
Washington does the big jobs — money, war, treaties. States run daily life — schools, police, your license. Amendment ten leaves the rest to the states or the people.

Officeholder answers never freeze: the bank says visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates — answer for YOUR interview day: president, vice president, Speaker, Chief Justice, plus your own state's names.
V J R — Vote, Jury, Run for office: citizens only. But everyone's rights start with Freedom of — plus the right to bear arms.
Three doors in: born, naturalize, derive. The Oath in five beats: give up, defend, obey, serve, be loyal. The Pledge: loyalty to the flag and the United States.
Serve and participate: vote, pay taxes, obey the law. Men eighteen through twenty-five register for Selective Service — the law says so, and it keeps a draft fair.
American Indians were here FIRST. Africans were TAKEN as slaves. The colonists came chasing FREEDOM.
Seventeen seventy-six — declare: July fourth. Taxation without representation lit the fire; the Revolution ran from Bunker Hill to Yorktown. Chant the thirteen coastal colonies, north to south.
The Founders map: Washington the Country's father, Madison the Constitution's father, Jefferson the Writer, Hamilton the Treasurer, Franklin the man of firsts.
Seventeen eighty-seven — construct: the Constitution. Sold to the people by Madison, Hamilton, and Jay, writing as Publius.

When in doubt in the eighteen hundreds: Civil War — North versus South, the war that ended slavery. Lincoln the sixteenth freed the slaves and saved the Union. And eighteen-oh-three: Louisiana doubled the map.
The amendment ladder: thirteen free, fourteen citizen, fifteen vote — all men by eighteen seventy. Susan B. Anthony — B for Ballot.
World War One: Germany attacked our ships. World War Two: Pearl Harbor. Eisenhower: the general who became president.
One storyline: the nineteen twenty-nine crash, the longest recession in modern history, and Franklin Roosevelt leading through Depression and war.
The Cold War cluster: the rival is the Soviet Union, and Korea, Vietnam, and the Cold War worry all share one spoken answer — communism.
Nineteenth Amendment, nineteen twenty: women vote. King fought for civil rights; the movement fought to end racial discrimination.
Nine-eleven: terrorists attacked the United States — then the War on Terror. Say a tribe you know: Cherokee, Navajo, Sioux. American ideas: the light bulb, the airplane, the moon.
